title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Vitruvius removes a heavier floating stone before a lighter gold trial sinks in the same quicksilver setup
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED_NO_MEANING_CLAIM. Complete cached Vitruvius VII.8 §3 offers a conditional sequential comparison: quicksilver in a vessel supports a hundred-pound stone; after removing that weight, a scruple of gold is put on and sinks rather than swimming. Its conclusion distinguishes substance nature from amount of weight. Preserve distinct trial participants, explicit removal-before-replacement, opposite outcome polarity and the source mass ordering. This is a new raw source-duty candidate rather than equal-mass crown assay, gold recovery or covered-jar metal production.

design.mechanism: A persistent quicksilver/vessel setup supports two conditional trials separated by removal of the first load. The heavier stone has floating and three negative liquid-disruption outcomes; the much lighter gold has not-floating and sinking outcomes. The argument rejects amount-of-weight alone as the explanation, invoking substance nature.
design.unit: Complete Vitruvius VII.8 sections1–4; operative conditional comparison and conclusion section3.
design.contrast: Sequential heavier-stone-floats / lighter-gold-sinks versus a greater-load-implies-sinking account, simultaneous two-load addition, or one object changing from stone into gold. Unlike751, inputs are explicitly unequal in weight; unlike756, the source duty is a conditional comparison rather than extraction/separation.
design.prediction: Before target selection, freeze one signed floating/sinking predicate, subject slots, removal-and-replacement event order and source mass inequality. Any later whole-context candidate claiming this duty must realize opposing outcomes on two distinct successive participants under fixed predicate meanings, with removal scoped to the first participant and put-on scoped to the second. Reverse participant attachment, simultaneous accumulation, transformation of the stone into gold, or heavier-implies-sinks contradict this source account. A mere pair of different material names or free thirteen-gloss paragraph does not meet the duty. No target selected or read; these constraints do not identify which existing wordforms carry them.
design.scope: Historical argument-structure raw proposal only, conditional source assertion not performed experiment or modern buoyancy law. No universal mass-to-motion rule or inherited gloss; no claim to reopen751/756/836 or choose a Voynich source/language.

source_evidence.quote:
CHAPTER VIII
CINNABAR AND QUICKSILVER
1. I shall now proceed to explain the nature of cinnabar. It is said
that it was first found in the Cilbian country belonging to Ephesus, and
both it and its properties are certainly very strange. First, before
getting to the vermilion itself by methods of treatment, they dig out
what is called the clod, an ore like iron, but rather of a reddish
colour and covered with a red dust. During the digging it sheds, under
the blows of the tools, tear after tear of quicksilver, which is at once
gathered up by the diggers.
2. When these clods have been collected, they are so full of moisture
that they are thrown into an oven in the laboratory to dry, and the
fumes that are sent up from them by the heat of the fire settle down on
the floor of the oven, and are found to be quicksilver. When the clods
are taken out, the drops which remain are so small that they cannot be
gathered up, but they are swept into a vessel of water, and there they
run together and combine into one. Four pints of it, when measured and
weighed, will be found to be one hundred pounds.
3. If the quicksilver is poured into a vessel, and a stone weighing one
hundred pounds is laid upon it, the stone swims on the surface, and
cannot depress the liquid, nor break through, nor separate it. If we
remove the hundred pound weight, and put on a scruple of gold, it will
not swim, but will sink to the bottom of its own accord. Hence, it is
undeniable that the gravity of a substance depends not on the amount of
its weight, but on its nature.
4. Quicksilver is a useful thing for many purposes. For instance,
neither silver nor copper can be gilded properly without it. And when
gold has been woven into a garment, and the garment becomes worn out
with age so that it is no longer respectable to use, the pieces of cloth
are put into earthen pots, and burned up over a fire. The ashes are then
thrown into water and[216] quicksilver added thereto. This attracts all the
bits of gold, and makes them combine with itself. The water is then
poured off, and the rest emptied into a cloth and squeezed in the hands,
whereupon the quicksilver, being a liquid, escapes through the loose
texture of the cloth, but the gold, which has been brought together by
the squeezing, is found inside in a pure state.

assumptions_and_limits: The source is an historical English translation of ancient prose, not diplomatic Latin or an identified medieval manuscript source.
Conditionals describe a proposed comparison; no claim the recorded source performed a modern controlled trial.
The stone is removed before gold is put on. The source does not independently specify replacing the quicksilver or refilling/resetting the vessel.
The text names unequal quantities, not equal-volume or equal-mass inputs. Do not borrow crown-assay751 refilling/volume duties.
The conclusion uses nature rather than amount of weight; no numerical density formula, generic physical law, alloy/amalgam state or molecular account is supplied.
Source section2 four-pint/hundred-pound quicksilver measure is a separate clause; no volume of the section3 setup specified.
Source section4 gold recovery756 remains distinct; its extraction, mixture, squeezed cloth and purified gold are not imported into this trial.
